headline: Strait of Hormuz Crisis Drives WTI Above $100 as Canada Posts 0.1% GDP Growth and 84,000 Job Losses
executive_summary:
WTI crude oil settled at US$102.88/bbl on March 30 — the first close above $100 since July 2022 — as the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz since approximately March 2 continued to disrupt an estimated 20 million barrels per day of global seaborne oil flows, representing roughly 20% of world trade.27 Brent crude surged approximately 55% in March to US$112.78/bbl, a record monthly gain since the contract's 1988 inception.27 The Dallas Federal Reserve estimated that a one-quarter closure of the strait could raise the WTI average to $98/bbl and reduce global GDP growth by an annualized 2.9 percentage points in Q2 2026.37 The project database tracks 63 oil and gas projects and 785 power and energy projects across Canada, with Alberta accounting for 727 of all tracked projects.

Statistics Canada's Labour Force Survey recorded employment falling by 84,000 positions (-0.4%) in February 2026, reversing gains accumulated through Q4 2025.12 Full-time employment fell 108,000 and private-sector employment declined 73,000. The unemployment rate rose to 6.7%, up 0.2 percentage points from January, while the participation rate edged down 0.1 percentage points to 64.9%.12 Services-producing industries shed 56,000 positions; goods-producing industries lost 28,000, with wholesale and retail trade recording the largest subsector decline at 18,000 jobs. The database tracks 1,034 projects currently under construction that operate within active labour markets.

Real GDP rose 0.1% in January 2026, a second consecutive monthly increase following a flat December.4 Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction expanded 1.2%, while manufacturing contracted 1.4% due to weakness across both durable and non-durable goods.4 Statistics Canada's advance estimate for February points to 0.2% growth. Headline CPI decelerated to 1.8% year-over-year in February, down from 2.3% in January — the lowest reading since early 2021 — with all three core measures converging near the Bank of Canada's 2% target.8 The Bank of Canada held the overnight rate at 2.25% on March 18, citing weaker near-term growth from US tariffs and stating the Governing Council would proceed carefully given heightened uncertainty.1

Canada's merchandise trade deficit widened to $3.6 billion in January from $1.3 billion in December.18 Motor vehicle and parts exports dropped 21.2% to $5.4 billion — the lowest since September 2021 — while energy exports partially offset the decline, rising 4.1%.18 The federal government and Ontario signed an $8.8 billion cost-matched housing deal reducing municipal development charges by up to 50% and removing HST on new homes valued up to $1 million.16 Housing starts ran at 250,900 SAAR in February, up 4.5% from January.15

The April 2 release of February merchandise trade data will be the first full-month reading following the Strait of Hormuz closure initiation. Statistics Canada releases the March Labour Force Survey on April 3.43 The Bank of Canada delivers its next rate decision on April 15, alongside the Monetary Policy Report and the March CPI release — the most data-dense event in the near-term calendar.2

national.analysis:
Statistics Canada reported real GDP grew 0.1% in January 2026, marking a second consecutive monthly increase following a flat December 2025.4 Goods-producing industries expanded 0.2% for the second straight month, driven by mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction, which posted a 1.2% monthly gain.4 Construction also contributed to goods-sector growth in January. Services-producing industries were essentially unchanged: retail trade GDP rose 0.8% and finance and insurance offset declines in wholesale trade and transportation and warehousing.4 Manufacturing contracted 1.4% in January — reflecting weakness in both durable and non-durable goods production.4 Statistics Canada's advance estimate for February 2026 indicates 0.2% growth, which would represent the third consecutive monthly gain. On a quarterly basis, Q4 2025 real GDP contracted 0.2% annualized, following a 0.6% gain in Q3 2025. Full-year 2025 GDP growth was approximately 1.7%; the IMF projects 1.6% for 2026.67 The database tracks 49 manufacturing projects, 364 mining projects, and 63 oil and gas projects connected to these industry-level GDP movements.

The labour market recorded a broad contraction in February. Statistics Canada's Labour Force Survey showed employment declining 84,000 (-0.4%) — reversing the 76,000 gain in January.12 Full-time employment fell 108,000 while part-time employment increased 24,000. Private-sector employment declined 73,000; public-sector employment edged up 2,000 and self-employment declined 13,000.12 The unemployment rate rose to 6.7%, up 0.2 percentage points from January's 6.5%, and the participation rate declined 0.1 percentage points to 64.9%.12 The employment decline was broad-based: services-producing industries shed 56,000 positions, with wholesale and retail trade losing 18,000 and other services declining 14,000. Goods-producing industries lost 28,000.1213 The separate Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours (SEPH) recorded payroll employment rising 45,600 (+0.2%) in January 2026, providing a divergent signal from the household-based Labour Force Survey for that month.14 The March 2026 Labour Force Survey is scheduled for release on April 3.

Headline CPI decelerated to 1.8% year-over-year in February 2026, down from 2.3% in January — the lowest reading since early 2021, and slightly below market expectations of 1.9%.8 All three Bank of Canada core measures converged in February: CPI-median at 2.3%, CPI-trim at 2.3%, and CPI-common at 2.4%.8 Food inflation decelerated to 5.3% from 7.3% in January, driven in part by base effects from the February 2025 GST/HST tax break expiry. Shelter, recreation, education, and household operations costs also decelerated.9 March is the final month affected by the GST/HST base-year effect; the March CPI release is scheduled for April 15, coinciding with the Bank of Canada's rate decision and Monetary Policy Report.11 The Bank of Canada held the overnight rate at 2.25% on March 18 — the seventh consecutive meeting at this level, following seven cuts from the June 2024 peak of 5.00%.1 Bond markets priced approximately 86% probability of no change at the April 15 meeting and approximately 14% probability of a 25-basis-point hike.3 The database tracks 211 residential projects sensitive to rate and inflation dynamics.

Canada's merchandise trade deficit widened to $3.6 billion in January 2026, from $1.3 billion in December 2025.18 Total exports fell 4.7% to $62.5 billion; imports declined 1.1% to $66.1 billion. Motor vehicle and parts exports dropped 21.2% to $5.4 billion — the lowest since September 2021 — linked to lower Canadian motor vehicle production.18 Energy product exports partially offset the decline, rising 4.1%, led by natural gas.18 US tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum remain in effect; the Bank of Canada cited these trade disruptions as contributing to weaker near-term growth projections.1 The database tracks 600 transport and logistics projects and 49 manufacturing projects exposed to cross-border trade conditions. February merchandise trade data — the first full month following the Strait of Hormuz closure — is scheduled for release April 2.45

Housing starts ran at 250,900 units SAAR in February 2026, up 4.5% from 240,148 in January. The six-month trend declined 0.4% to 256,005 units; CMHC noted the trend remains relatively steady despite monthly volatility.15 The national average home price rose to $663,828 in February, up 1.7% month-over-month, while the MLS HPI benchmark increased to $661,300, ending a decline observed through late 2025.16 Fixed mortgage rates held firm or increased due to elevated long-term Government of Canada bond yields, while variable rates declined in line with BoC cuts.16 Retail sales rose 1.1% to $70.7 billion in January, with motor vehicle and parts dealers leading at +2.0% and general merchandise retailers posting a fourth consecutive monthly increase at +3.0%.40 Statistics Canada's advance estimate for February retail sales is +0.9%, subject to revision. E-commerce sales rose 1.5% to $4.4 billion, representing 6.2% of total retail trade.41

industry_executive_summary:
Canada's goods and services sectors face divergent pressures. Manufacturing PMI expanded to 51.0 in February, signalling renewed factory expansion, while raw materials prices climbed 8.6% year-over-year on crude oil, agriculture, and base metals strength.2,4 Services sectors showed resilience: retail trade (January) reflected consumer spending despite tariff constraints, while defence-bank initiatives and quantum technology signal emerging growth vectors.5,6 The goods sector remains exposed to oil surge (WTI $102.88, Brent $112.57) while services benefit from labour scarcity and government support.2 Railway carloadings declined, reflecting softer goods movement and tariff disruptions.8

Within goods industries, energy and raw materials benefit from commodity strength while manufacturing faces input-cost pressures and tariff-driven demand constraints. Precious metals surged: silver climbed 115.7% year-over-year and platinum 100.4%, reflecting safe-haven demand on Iran tensions and geopolitical risks.2 Base metals also strengthened on stronger renminbi (USD/CNY 6.90) supporting Canadian export competitiveness to China, though slowing Chinese growth creates offsetting pressure.2 Construction remains tepid with 250,900 housing starts in February (up 4.8% monthly but six-month trend flat), indicating caution despite policy accommodation.3

Services sectors—defence, innovation, professional services—receive support from government spending and persistent labour scarcity despite headline unemployment of 6.7%. Retail trade maintained momentum despite employment losses and cross-border travel collapse (down 22.0% year-over-year), indicating consumers prioritize necessities and strategic purchases while retracting discretionary spending.5,7 The sectoral divergence reflects structural shifts: goods sectors dependent on cross-border supply chains face tariff frictions, while services insulated from trade barriers benefit from government investment in defence, innovation, and education.1
consumer_pulse:
The Conference Board of Canada's consumer confidence index declined to 47.50 points in February 2026, down from 49.30 in January.38 The Bloomberg/Nanos Canadian Confidence Index showed a three-week slide into late March, moving from a modestly positive position toward neutrality. Nanos Research reported that the proportion of Canadians who believe the economy will strengthen over the next six months rose from 17% to 26% over a four-week period — a shift in forward expectations alongside current caution.39

Retail sales rose 1.1% to $70.7 billion in January 2026, with motor vehicle and parts dealers leading gains at +2.0% after a 1.6% decline in December.40 General merchandise retailers posted a fourth consecutive monthly increase at +3.0%; core retail sales excluding gasoline and motor vehicles increased 0.9%. E-commerce rose 1.5% to $4.4 billion, accounting for 6.2% of total retail trade. Alberta recorded the largest provincial retail gain at +3.5%, led by motor vehicle sales. Gasoline station sales declined 0.4%.40 Statistics Canada's advance estimate for February retail sales is +0.9%.41

Online discussion and search data tracked in the week of March 24–30 reflect two distinct currents. The Strait of Hormuz crisis, oil prices above $100, US tariffs, job losses, and energy costs were the highest-frequency topics, all carrying negative sentiment scores. Partially offsetting signals — food inflation deceleration, motor vehicle sales strength, the $8.8 billion federal-Ontario housing deal, and the advance GDP growth estimate for February — registered at lower frequency with positive or neutral sentiment scores. Rising energy costs and US trade friction were the primary themes in ongoing consumer discussions.2712

commodities.name: WTI Crude Oil
commodities.commentary: WTI Crude Oil: US$102.88/bbl (+5.5% week-over-week) — the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz since approximately March 2, disrupting an estimated 20 million barrels per day (~20% of global seaborne oil flows), drove WTI to its first settlement above US$100 since July 2022; tanker traffic through the strait dropped approximately 70%1. The Dallas Fed estimated that a one-quarter closure could raise WTI to a US$98/bbl average and reduce global GDP growth by an annualized 2.9 percentage points in Q2 20265. The database tracks 42 oil and gas projects ($93.8 billion) across Canada, concentrated in Alberta oil sands and offshore Newfoundland and Labrador2. WTI is up approximately 50% month-over-month1.

commodities.name: Western Canadian Select
commodities.commentary: Western Canadian Select: US$87.14/bbl — the WCS-WTI differential is estimated at US$15.74/bbl, reflecting the ongoing cost disadvantage for Canadian heavy crude producers relative to the West Texas benchmark3. The database tracks 42 oil and gas projects ($93.8 billion) across Alberta and Saskatchewan in which producer netback prices reference WCS-linked pricing2. Pipeline capacity through the expanded Trans Mountain system partially constrains the differential from widening further3.

commodities.name: Brent Crude
commodities.commentary: Brent Crude: US$112.57/bbl — Brent surged approximately 55% in March, a record monthly gain for the contract since its inception in 1988, as the Strait of Hormuz disruption rippled through global oil markets1. Brent peaked at approximately US$126/bbl intra-month before retreating on reports of potential US-Iran diplomatic talks1. The Brent-WTI spread of approximately US$9.69/bbl reflects elevated Atlantic Basin demand and longer tanker routing via the Cape of Good Hope.

commodities.name: Natural Gas (Henry Hub)
commodities.commentary: Natural Gas (Henry Hub): US$2.94/MMBtu — Henry Hub and the Canadian AECO benchmark rose as global LNG demand spiked in response to Middle East supply disruptions6. The EIA's March 10 short-term energy outlook projected Henry Hub averaging US$3.80/MMBtu for full-year 20266. The database tracks 317 power and energy projects ($487 billion), including BC LNG infrastructure and Alberta natural gas processing facilities, affected by shifting gas price levels2.

commodities.name: Gold
commodities.commentary: Gold: US$4,578/oz — gold declined more than 14% in March, on pace for its steepest monthly decline since October 2008, as margin liquidation and US dollar strength drove sellers despite elevated geopolitical tensions4. Gold peaked at approximately US$5,161/oz on March 3 before retreating. The database tracks mining projects across BC, Ontario, and Quebec that reference gold price levels in feasibility parameters2.

commodities.name: Silver
commodities.commentary: Silver: US$73.33/oz — silver tracked the broader precious metals retreat in March alongside gold's margin-driven decline4. Ontario and BC silver mining operations factor into the database's tracked mining project inventory2.

commodities.name: Copper
commodities.commentary: Copper: US$5.76/lb — copper held in an elevated range of US$5.25–$6.01/lb in March, reflecting mixed signals from China's manufacturing PMI recovery to 50.4 in March and global supply chain disruption from Middle East instability7,8. BC and Ontario copper mining projects tracked in the database reference price levels above the current spot for long-run feasibility thresholds2. Electrification-driven demand across grid and EV supply chain investment in Canada continues to support copper's demand profile7.

commodities.name: Aluminum
commodities.commentary: Aluminum: US$3,423/MT — aluminum prices reflect elevated energy input costs following the Strait of Hormuz supply disruption, given the metal's energy-intensive smelting process1. Canadian aluminum production, concentrated in Quebec smelting operations, contributes to export volumes subject to ongoing US tariff measures9.

commodities.name: Lumber
commodities.commentary: Lumber: US$610/MBF — live lumber price data has been unavailable from the primary timeseries data source since May 2023 due to a ticker or data feed issue; the US$610/MBF figure is sourced from the task brief10. BC forestry operations and residential construction projects in the database — including 211 residential projects tracked nationally — use lumber as a primary input cost benchmark2.

commodities.name: Uranium
commodities.commentary: Uranium: US$92/lb — uranium declined approximately 17% month-over-month alongside broader risk-off sentiment in metals; the URA ETF proxy fell to US$46.86 and Cameco (CCO.TO) closed at C$147.75, down approximately 14% month-over-month4. Saskatchewan is home to the majority of Canada's uranium production, including Cameco operations at Cigar Lake and McArthur River2.

commodities.name: Nickel
commodities.commentary: Nickel: US$14,641/MT (US$6.64/lb) — nickel moved under pressure in March as battery supply chain demand signals from China's manufacturing sector remained mixed despite the PMI returning above 508. Ontario (Vale, Glencore), Manitoba, and Labrador nickel mining operations link to the database's tracked mineral project inventory2.

commodities.name: Canola
commodities.commentary: Canola: C$733/MT — Prairie canola pricing reflects export demand conditions with China as a primary destination, subject to ongoing bilateral trade dynamics9. Saskatchewan and Alberta crushing capacity and oilseed storage infrastructure projects tracked in the database reference canola throughput volumes2.

commodities.name: Potash
commodities.commentary: Potash: US$355/MT — Nutrien (NTR.TO) traded at approximately C$104.62, down 1.0% week-over-week and up 1.0% month-over-month, indicating broadly stable potash benchmark pricing4. Saskatchewan potash operations, including Nutrien and Mosaic production sites, account for approximately 30% of global potash supply and link to several extraction projects in the database2.

commodities.name: Iron Ore
commodities.commentary: Iron Ore: price data not obtained in the current data refresh period — no current figure available from the tracked timeseries2. Iron ore pricing affects Quebec and Labrador iron ore pellet operations, including those linked to the Labrador Trough mining corridor tracked in the project database2.

yieldCurve.yield_commentary: The Government of Canada yield curve maintained a normal shape in the week ending March 30, with the 2–10 year spread at 63 basis points — the 10-year yield stood at 3.58% against the 2-year at 2.95%.4 Across the full curve: the 3-month at 2.28%, the 1-year at 2.55%, the 5-year at 3.18%, the 20-year at 3.85%, and the 30-year at 3.94%.4 Year-over-year, the belly and long end rose: the 2-year is up 33 basis points from 2.62%, the 10-year up 36 basis points from 3.22%, while the 3-month fell 122 basis points from 3.50% as the Bank of Canada completed seven consecutive cuts from the June 2024 peak of 5.00%.45 The database tracks 2,739 projects in proposed or approved status in rate-sensitive sectors, including 211 residential and 68 commercial-mixed projects.3

  • Wheat futures settled at $586.00 per bushel and soybeans at $1,158.50, providing Canadian crop producers with elevated price signals relative to recent historical norms, supporting farm revenue despite the volume dip.7

  • NAICS 111 (Crop Production) and NAICS 112 (Animal Production) are the primary sub-sectors; the monthly dip likely reflects seasonal inventory drawdown rather than a structural reversal given the robust year-over-year base.1
  • Canada's interprovincial trade in manufactured goods — closely linked to agri-food processing — rose just 0.7% to $167.4 billion in 2024, suggesting limited downstream pull for raw agricultural inputs.8

China's National Bureau of Statistics reported the official manufacturing PMI rose to 50.4 in March 2026, crossing above the 50.0 expansion threshold after two months of contraction (49.3 in January, 49.0 in February).35 The non-manufacturing PMI increased to 50.1 from 49.5, with new export orders showing strength in the March reading. The People's Bank of China held the 5-year Loan Prime Rate at 2.90%. China recorded GDP growth of 5.0% for full-year 2025, meeting the official annual target. CPI registered +0.2% year-over-year in February, reflecting subdued domestic demand. Higher shipping costs and elevated imported commodity prices from the Middle East conflict weighed on input prices for surveyed manufacturers.35

China is Canada's second-largest merchandise trading partner, receiving approximately 5% of Canadian merchandise exports annually — crude oil, canola, potash, wood products, and seafood are the primary export categories. The return of manufacturing PMI to expansion after two months of contraction affects demand signals for these Canadian commodity exports through Q2 2026. The Strait of Hormuz closure has raised transport costs for Canadian LNG and commodity shipments routed to Asia via the Indian Ocean.36 China controls an estimated 60% of global rare earth mine production and approximately 85% of downstream rare earth processing, a factor relevant to the 364 mining projects tracked in the Canadian database, particularly those targeting critical minerals for battery and defence supply chains.

market_commentary:
Canadian financial markets closed March with a broad rally on March 31 — the S&P/TSX Composite rose 1.54% on the day to 32,4271 after reports of potential US-Iran diplomatic talks, though the index still declined approximately 6% over the month as the Strait of Hormuz closure — effective since approximately March 2 — drove energy supply disruption across global markets. WTI crude settled at $102.88/bbl on March 30, the first settlement above $100 since July 2022 and a gain of more than 50% in March2; Brent reached $112.78/bbl, a record monthly gain for that contract since 1988. The Bank of Canada held its overnight rate at 2.25% on March 183, and the Canadian dollar closed at 0.7198 USD, down 1.85% month-over-month despite elevated crude prices4.

The project pipeline's commodity exposure diverged sharply along energy lines — the database tracks 42 oil_gas projects ($93.8B) and 317 power_energy projects ($487B) whose development economics intersect with the crude price environment5. The 10-year Government of Canada bond yield stood at 3.58%, up 36 basis points year-over-year, with the 2-10 spread at 63 basis points; the database contains 211 residential projects in proposed or planning stages that carry financing cost exposure to the yield curve5. Gold declined 14% in March to $4,578/oz from a peak of $5,161 on March 3, driven by margin liquidation and US dollar appreciation6; the database tracks 364 mining projects across Canada with precious-metals exposure.

wcs_analysis.analysis_text: The Western Canadian Select differential to WTI was approximately US$15.74/bbl in the week ending March 30, 2026. At the current WCS netback, Canadian heavy crude producers receive US$87.14/bbl before transportation and processing costs. The database tracks 42 oil and gas projects ($93.8 billion) for which WCS-linked producer pricing is a key economic input. Pipeline capacity through the expanded Trans Mountain system provides an export corridor to tidewater that partially constrains discount widening relative to historical pre-TMX levels.

commodity_commentary: Canadian-relevant commodities diverged sharply across categories in the week ending March 30, 2026 — energy prices advanced across the board, with WTI crude crossing US$100/bbl for the first time since July 2022 on the continued Strait of Hormuz disruption, while precious metals retreated, with gold down 14% month-over-month despite elevated geopolitical tensions, driven by margin liquidation and a stronger US dollar1,4. The WCS-WTI discount narrowed to an estimated US$15.74/bbl, holding at a historical spread for Canadian heavy crude producers3. Base metals were mixed, with copper elevated at US$5.76/lb and nickel under pressure, while uranium declined on risk-off sentiment7. The database tracks 42 oil and gas projects ($93.8 billion) and 317 power energy projects ($487 billion) linked to commodity price levels across Canada2.
